1.x: “his own city”: Capernaum. Jesus had just left there to get away from the crowds for a time.

2.x: “Jesus seeing their faith”: Jesus did not see their work, rather the faith that led them to come to him. What saves us is always the faith, not the works we do. The physical effort required to carry a person to Jesus was a practical manifestation of their internal faith. Also, the faith of everyone (“their faith”) helped this paralytic man, showing how our faith can positively affect others. While the man was brought for physical restoration, Jesus’ first words address his spiritual state. By saying “thy sins are forgiven”, Jesus suggests that the weight of the soul is of greater primary concern than the mobility of the body. “Son”: Jesus calls him Son because he is our Father: “I[Jesus] will not leave you as orphans(without a Father)” (Jn 14:18 BSB). He is our “Eternal Father” (Isa 9:6). “Thy sins are forgiven”: As the only true God (Jn 17:3) in the flesh (Col 2:8-9; 2 Cor 5:19), Jesus can forgive sins because he is the same YHWH of the OT: “I, even I, am He who blots out your transgressions.. and remembers your sins no more” (Isa 43:25 KJV). Sicknesses are sometimes due to sin (for example the believers getting weak, sick, and even dying because they took the Lord’s Supper in an unworthy manner in 1 Cor 11:27-30; or David’s son dying due to David’s sin with Bathsheba in 2 Sam 12:13-18, or John telling a healed man: “sin no more, lest a worse thing come upon you” in Jn 5:14), and sometimes are not (for example Jesus saying the man is sick so that the works of God should be revealed in him in Jn 9:1-3, or the story of Job).

3.x: The religious leaders (the scribes) were experts in Jewish law. To them, Jesus’ claim was the ultimate “red flag.” In Jewish theology, sin was an offense against God; therefore, only God had the right to forgive it (Mk 2:7). By claiming to forgive the man’s sins, Jesus was (in their eyes) claiming the status of deity.

4.x: Here Jesus demonstrates omniscience (knowing their private thoughts). He provides the first piece of evidence that he is operating on a level far above a standard teacher. It is important to clarify that omniscience comes from the divine Spirit (the Father) dwelling in Jesus (Col 2:8-9; 2 Cor 5:19), not from the Son (the human). The Son is not omniscient, he does not know the hour (Mt 24:36). A Trinitarian believes Jesus is a standalone God (the 2nd person of the Trinity that shares the divine essence of God with other two persons). Therefore, they believe the Son purposely “made himself nothing” (emptied himself, Phil 2:7) of his divine powers, yet, he could still have flares of divine attributes, like his healings and moments of omniscience. As a Oneness, I see that belief wanting because: (1) if Jesus loses his divine attributes (like omnipresence, omniscience) then he literally cease to be God; (2) if Jesus chooses when to remain ignorant and when to remain powerless, then it’s all one big game for him, and there is no sacrifice in his obedience. The Bible harmonizes a lot better when we understand the Son is not God, but that the Son is the dwelling place & image of the invisible Father. A Trinitarian believes in three hypostasis (persons) and one ousia (one essence, nature, being). However, the Bible says that Jesus is “the express image of His(the Father’s) person(hypostasis)” (Heb 1:3 KJV). There is only one divine hypostasis(person), and Jesus is the image of that one divine person, not a second divine person (as Trinitarians claim). The term “God-the-Son” is unbiblical. The man Jesus is the Son OF God & the Lamb OF God, but he is not God-the-Son nor God-the-Lamb for God does not die, nor has bones and flesh.

7.x: The healed man didn’t just twitch or sit up; he undergoes a complete restoration. He picks up the very mat he was carried in on and walks home. The physical movement serves as the “receipt” for his spiritual forgiveness.

8.x: Unlike the scribes, who were preoccupied with theological technicalities and concerns about blasphemy, “the multitudes” responded with two distinct actions: (1) “marvelled” (awe): they were struck by the sheer wonder of the event. They recognized that something supernatural had just occurred; (2) “glorified God”: they recognized the source of the miracle. They correctly attributed the healing to God, acknowledging that the power displayed was a divine act. However, they misunderstood something. The crowd says that God had given such power “unto men” (plural). While they were correct that the power came from God, they still struggled to grasp the full identity of Jesus. They viewed him similar to the prophets of the OT who performed miracles by God’s authority. They did not yet fully realize that Jesus was not merely receiving power from God, but was operating as God in human form.

“Had given such power unto men”: Catholicism teaches that this verse shows the Sacrament of Reconciliation. That after Jesus’ resurrection, Jesus invests other men (apostles) with the same power to forgive sins in his name (Jn 20:23; Mt 18:18; CCC 1441, 1444, Ignatius Catholic Study Bible). This teaching comes from taking Jn 20:23 out of context. Jn 20:22-23 KJV says: “And when he had said this, he breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost: Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained.” By simply reading this verse by itself, it makes sense why someone might think that the apostles were given the authority to forgive sins. However, by taking the context of the entire Bible, that teaching is erroneous. THERE IS NOT A SINGLE INSTANCE OF THE APOSTLES FORGIVING SINS IN THE BIBLE, rather they were given the authority to PREACH FORGIVENESS OF SINS. First, the only sins that we can forgive are the ones done against us, but only God can forgive sins committed against Him: “If thy brother trespass AGAINST THEE, rebuke him; and if he repent, FORGIVE HIM” (Lk 17:3 KJV); “Then came PETER to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother SIN AGAINST ME, and I FORGIVE HIM? Till seven times?” (Mt 18:21 KJV); “Our Father which art in heaven… forgive us our sins; FOR WE ALSO FORGIVE EVERY ONE THAT IS INDEBTED TO US” (Lk 11:2,4 KJV). Even Peter, when he had the chance to put in practice this “power to forgive sins” (this happened AFTER Jesus had ascended), he did not forgive sins, but redirected to God: “Repent.. And PRAY GOD, if perhaps the thought in thine heart may be forgiven thee” (Acts 8:22 KJV). If Peter had the authority to forgive sins, why did he redirect Simon to God instead of him? What does it mean then, for the apostles to have the authority to “remit” and “retain” sins? The easiest way to understand John 20:21-23, is to realize that it has parallel passages. The Bible interprets itself, so if a verse is confusing, in order to understand it we have to begin by reading the immediate context, the overall Biblical context, and any parallel passages. The immediate context is Jesus' first post-resurrection appearance to the disciples and giving them the Great Commission: “as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you” (v.21 KJV). He empowers the apostles: “Receive ye the Holy Ghost” (v.22 KJV); and gives them authority to “remit” and “retain” sin (v 23). We now discover that Matthew 28, Mark 16, Luke 24, & John 20 ARE PARALLEL CHAPTERS. They all talk about the same events, beginning from the women finding the empty tomb, to Jesus giving his disciples the Great Commission. Keep in mind, the Great Commission is repeated multiple times, at Mount Galilee in Mt 28:16 and at Jerusalem in Lk 24:49 & John 20:19, however, the message is the same. To understand John 20:21-23, we just need to read its parallel passage in Luke 24:45-49. So here are the two parallel passages: (1) “Peace be unto you… Then OPENED HE THEIR UNDERSTANDING, that they might understand the scriptures, And said unto them, Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day: AND THAT REPENTANCE and REMISSION OF SINS should be PREACHED in his name AMONG ALL NATIONS, beginning in Jerusalem” (L 24:36,45-47 KJV) & (2) “Peace be unto you: as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you.And when he had said this, HE BREATHED ON THEM, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost: Whose soever sins ye REMIT, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye RETAIN, they are retained” (Jn 20:21-23 KJV). By harmonizing both versions of the Great Commission, we see that “opening their understanding” in Luke is equivalent to Jesus “breathing on them the Holy Spirit”. Especially since this cannot mean that the apostles received the Holy Spirit baptism, since that occurred for the first time at Pentecost in Acts 2:1-4. And we also see that to “remit” and to “retain” sins refers to “preaching repentance and remission of sins.” Hence, when they preach Christ, they “remit” sins, but when we deprive people of the gospel, they “retain” sin. John 20:21-23 does not give the apostles the power to forgive sins (much less to pass that power down to Roman Priests millennia later), but he gives them the Great Commission to go to ALL NATIONS to preach the gospel of forgiveness of sins. Soon after the Great Commission, Jesus ascends into heaven, and the apostles are left alone to carry out Jesus’ Commission. THEY DO NOT GO ABOUT FORGIVING SINS, BUT PREACHING THE FORGIVENESS OF SINS. Starting with Peter in Acts 2:38, where he shares the gospel for the first time to the Jews: “Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the REMISSION OF SINS, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost” (Acts 2:38 KJV). Then “Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is PREACHED UNTO YOU THE FORGIVENESS OF SINS” (Acts 13:38 KJV). The apostles were not even alone when Jesus appeared to them and commissioned them (Lk 24:33), hence, the preaching of forgiveness of sins is not solely an apostle's duty, but everyone’s duty. Just like how in the OT a priest could declare the lepers “clean” o “unclean”(Lev 13:3,6-8), likewise we can declare a person clean of sin if that person BELIEVED(faith), REPENTED, AND GOT BAPTIZED IN JESUS NAME (Acts 2:38; 22:16) (we cannot say they’re forgiven if they haven’t followed Scripture, as many non-biblical traditions of man falsely promise forgiveness of sins without repentance, faith, or water baptism in Jesus’ name). Also, notice that it did not mean that the OT priests had the power to clean leprosy (God was the one doing the healing, they simply would confirm), God is the only one who can forgive sins committed against His law (Mk 2:7) and God specifically tell us to ask forgiveness of sins to Him directly (Ps 51:1-2;32:5;25:11; Mt 6:9,12; Lk 11:4; 1 Jn 1:9; Acts 8:22; etc). Our ONLY mediator between God and men is Jesus (1 Tim 2:5). “If anyone sins, we have an ADVOCATE with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 Jn 2:1 KJV). Only Jesus has a sacrifice to show for our sin. Those fake human priests today do not have anything to show for our sin before God. God fulfilled the sacrificial priesthood, and in case the Bible wasn’t clear enough, He destroyed the Jewish temple in 70AC. Yet, fake religions keep trying to place human mediators between us and God to make people dependent on their institution. The moment Jesus died, the veil that separated the Holy place from the Holy of Holies was torn in two (Mt 27:50-51), giving us access directly to God: “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need” (Heb 4:16 KJV) & “Having thereforece… boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus… through the veil, that is to say, his flesh…let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith…” (Heb 10:19-22 KJV) & “In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him” (Eph 3:12 KJV).

9.x: The “receipt of custom” was essentially a tax office. In 1st-century Judea, tax collectors were social outcasts. They worked for the Roman occupiers and often padded their own pockets by overcharging their fellow Jews. They were viewed as both traitors and thieves. The fact that this gospel carries the name of a tax collector gives weight to the evidence that it truly came from someone who witnessed the living Jesus. Matthew’s response to follow Jesus was immediate. While the fishermen (Peter and Andrew) could technically return to their boats later, Matthew was walking away from a lucrative government position. Once he left his “receipt of custom,” he likely couldn’t go back.

10.x: “Sat at meat” refers to reclining at a table for a formal meal. In that culture, sharing a meal was a sign of intimacy, friendship, and acceptance. Matthew’s first act after following Jesus is to throw a party for his friends: other “publicans” (tax collectors) and “sinners” (people who did not strictly follow the Mosaic Law).

11.x: The Pharisees were the “separatists” of their day; their very name implies being “set apart.” To them, holiness was maintained by avoiding “uncleanness.” By eating with tax collectors, Jesus wasn’t just being friendly; in their view, he was contaminating his own spiritual purity. Notice they don’t ask Jesus directly, they try to sow doubt among his disciples.

12.x: “They that be whole”: This refers to healthy people. People that think that they have no spiritual need (the Pharisees). “They that are sick”: These people recognize their moral and spiritual failings (the sinners, all of us). Jesus defines his mission: A doctor doesn’t spend his day with healthy people; he goes where the disease is. If the Pharisees were as "healthy" as they claimed, they shouldn’t be offended that a doctor is doing his job. “I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (v.13): Jesus did not come to call those who think they are “righteous” (those who are self-satisfied and unaware of their sin) but instead came to call sinners: people who admit they are lost, broken, and in need of rescue. This does not mean that only “obvious sinners” are saved, but that salvation is for those who acknowledge their sin and repent, turning to Christ as their Savior rather than relying on their own “goodness.” Even Paul says: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief” (1 Tim 1:15 KJV).

13.x: Jesus issues a stinging rebuke by telling the “experts” of the law to “go and learn.” He quotes Hosea 6:6. Mercy over Ritual: God prefers a heart of compassion (mercy) over the mechanical performance of religious rituals and sacrifices. The Pharisees were obsessed with the “sacrifice” (the rules) but lacked the “mercy” (the love for the lost). “I am not come to call the righteous”: this is ironic, since Jesus knows no one is truly righteous (Rom 3:10), but he is addressing the Pharisee’s perception of themselves. Since they believed they were perfect, they had excluded themselves from the help he was offering: “Christ is become of no effect unto you, whosoever of you are justified by the law; ye are fallen from grace” (Gal 5:4 KJV).

14.x: The questions are no longer coming from the Pharisees, but from John’s disciples. They are confused because they see a massive difference between their ascetic, disciplined lifestyle and the “party atmosphere” surrounding Jesus. Fasting was a sign of mourning, repentance, and intense spiritual preparation. John the Baptist was a “desert preacher” who live da very austere life, and his disciples followed suit. They saw the Pharisees fasting twice a week and they were doing the same. To them, Jesus’ disciples looked a bit too.. Happy. THey were essentially asking: “if this is a serious spiritual movement, why is everyone eating and drinking?”

15.x: Jesus responds with a wedding metaphor. In Jewish culture, a wedding was the most joyful celebration possible, often lasting seven days. The Bridegroom: Jesus identifies himself as the groom. In the OT, God is often described as the “Husband” of Israel. By calling himself the bridegroom, Jesus is making another subtle claim to divinity. The Children of the bridechamber: These are the wedding guests or groomsmen (the disciples). The logic is that it is socially inappropriate (even offensive) to fast or mourn at a wedding. You don’t go to a reception and refuse to eat to show how “holy” you are; you celebrate the presence of the groom. Jesus acknowledges that fasting has a place, but it’s all about timing. While Jesus is physically present on earth, it is a season of celebration. The Kingdom of Heaven has arrived. However, Jesus says the bridegroom will be “taken from them.” This is a dark, prophetic hint at this coming crucifixion. Once he is gone, his followers will fast as they long for his return. Jesus is teaching them that spiritual disciplines (like fasting) aren’t just “rules” to be checked off; they must correspond to what God is doing in the moment. You don’t mourn when the Savior is standing right in front of you.

16.x: In the ancient world, fabrics were hand-woven. If you took a piece of new, unshrunk wool and sewed it as a patch onto an old, already-shrunken cloak, a disaster occurred the first time you washed it. The new patch would shrink, pulling away from the fragile old threads and creating an even bigger hole (“the rent”) than before. Jesus’ kingdom isn’t a “patch” for the old Pharisaical system. He didn’t come to just “fix” a few things in the legalistic tradition; he came to bring something entirely whole and new.

17.x: “Bottles” refers to wineskins made of animal hide. New wineskins were soft, supple, and elastic. As new wine fermented, it released gases. The new skin would stretch to accommodate the pressure. Old wineskin behaved differently. Over time, skins became brittle and hard. If you put fermenting “new wine” into an old, rigid skin, the pressure would cause the leather to crack and burst. You’d lose both the wine and the container. Jesus is explaining why his disciples aren’t fasting like the Pharisees or even John’s disciples. The old wineskin represents the old religious structure based on merit, rigid rituals, and the Mosaic Law as interpreted by the Pharisees. It was “stiff” and could not expand to hold the radical grace Jesus was offering. The new wine is the gospel: the message of grace, the presence of the Messiah, and the coming of the Holy Spirit. It is “fermenting,” active, and powerful. The new wineskin represents the new hearts of the believers and the new way of relating to God through faith rather than just external rules. You cannot force the joy and freedom of the gospel into the narrow, rigid containers of legalism. This section forms a complete “mini-biography” of Jesus’ authority: he has authority over physical sickness, authority over sin, authority to call the outcasts, and authority to redefine religion itself.

18.x: “a certain ruler”: parallel passages identify this ruler as Jairus, a ruler of the local synagogue (Mk 5:22;Lk 8:41). This is significant because, as a religious leader, he was part of the very establishment that was currently criticizing Jesus. However, his grief as a father overrode his social standing. He doesn’t just ask for a prayer; he states that his daughter is “even now dead” (or at the point of death, as clarified in parallel accounts). His faith is specific. He believes that Jesus lying his hands on his daughter will save her. He doesn’t say “maybe she will live,” but rather “she shall live.”

19.x: “Jesus arose”: This is a small but powerful detail. Jesus was in the middle of a deep teaching session (about the wineskins), but he immediately stops to respond to a cry for help. He doesn’t tell the rule to “make an appointment” or wait until the lecture is over, he answers promptly to a prayer in faith.

20.x: The woman had a chronic hemorrhage for twelve years. Under Levitical law (Lev 15:25-27), this made her “ritually unclean.” Anything she touched became unclean, and she was barred from the Temple. She was socially and spiritually isolated. Because of her uncleanness, she didn’t approach Jesus face-to-face like the ruler did. She came “behind him” in the crowd, hoping to receive healing without being noticed or causing a scene. She reached the “hem”, which is the tzitzit (the ritual tassels) at the corner of his garment (“hem” refers to the Greek word “kraspedon” meaning “a tassel of twisted wool”). These are ritual fringes or tassels attached to the four corners of a garment, commanded in the Torah as a visual reminder of God’s commandments (Num 15:37-41; Deut 22:12).

21.x: Faith means to act as if it were true. The faith of this woman was “action-oriented” because she truly believed that Jesus could heal her.

22.x: “Daughter”: Jesus is our Father (Isa 9:6; Jn 14:7-9; Col 2:8-9). He will not leave us as “ORPHANS” (aka without a Father) (Jn 14:18 BSB). “Jesus turned him about”: The man Jesus felt the power go out from him (as noted in Mk 5:30). The man Jesus, as the only begotten of the Father, has access to the divine Spirit “without limit” (Jn 3:34 BSB). Here, the divine Spirit healed the woman before the human acknowledged it. “Thy faith hath made thee whole”: Jesus clarifies that she was healed because of her faith, not because of any meritorious work. The Greek word for “Whole” is “sozo”, which can mean both “healed” or “saved” depending on the context. In this context, it most likely refers to her being “healed” of her disease.

23.x: In 1st-century Jewish culture, even the poorest families were expected to hire at least two flute players (minstrels) and one professional wailing woman for a funeral. For a “ruler” like Jairus, the crowd would have been large and the “noise” (lamentation) significant. The presence of these professional mourners confirms that, from a human perspective, the girl was undeniably dead.

24.x: “Not dead, but sleepeth”: Jesus isn’t misdiagnosing her; he is speaking from a divine perspective. To the Giver of Life, death is no more permanent or difficult to wake from than a nap. “They laughed him to scorn”: What Jesus had just said sounded biologically absurd. This laughter serves as a “legal witness” to the fact that the girl was truly dead before the miracle occurred.

25.x: Jesus removes the mockers before performing the miracle. He isn’t interested in a circus-like display for those who have already rejected him. According to Jewish Law, touching a corpse made on “unclean,” but Jesus’ holiness flows outward, bringing life rather than contracting defilement. “The maid arose”: this was not a slow recovery, it was immediate.

26.x: Despite Jesus often telling people to keep his miracles quiet, the news of someone being raised from the dead was impossible to contain. This miracle placed Jesus in the same category as the great prophets Elijah and Elisha, but with the added authority he had already claimed over sin.

27.x: Jesus is leaving the ruler’s house when he is pursued by two blind men. This passage highlights a new level of public recognition of Jesus’ identity and emphasizes the “filter” of faith. “Son of David”: this is the first time in Matthew’s gospel that Jesus is publicly addressed by this Messianic title. By calling him this, the blind men are declaring that they believe Jesus is the promised King from the line of David who would restore Israel. “Crying”: the men aren’t just asking, they’re crying (shouting) and “following” him. Despite their physical blindness, they “see” who Jesus is more clearly than the Pharisees do.

28.x: Jesus doesn’t heal them immediately in the streets. He waits until he is “into the house.” This tests their persistence, as they had to follow him through the crowd, likely bumping into people, to get to him. Jesus asks a direct question about their faith. He doesn’t ask if they are “good people” or if they have followed the law; he asks if they believe (faith).

32.x: “As they went out”: this shows the relentless pace of Jesus’ ministry. As soon as the blind men leave, another case arrives. The man is “dumb” (unable to speak), but Matthew is careful to note that this wasn’t a biological or medical issue like the previous healings. This was a spiritual condition: demonic possession that had robbed the man of his voice. Like the paralyzed man and the ruler’s daughter, this man is brought to Jesus by others. It highlights the importance of the community bringing the broken to the Healer.

33.x: Jesus restores the man’s ability to communicate and worship. The multitude recognizes this is unprecedented. Even with the history of the prophets like Moses or Elijah, the sheer frequency, variety, and ease of Jesus’ miracles lead them to conclude that “It was never so seen in Israel.”

34.x: The chapter reaches a dramatic climax. We see the ultimate rejection of Jesus by the religious elite. The Pharisees cannot deny the fact of the miracle (the man is clearly speaking), so they attempt to re-label the source. They claim Jesus is using “black magic” or is in league with Beelzebub (Satan). This is a pivotal moment of spiritual hardness. By attributing the work of the Holy Spirit to the devil, they are closing the door on their own ability to recognize the truth. “But the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men” (Mt 12:31 KJV). The “unforgivable sin” is not a one-time slip-up, but a hardened, deliberate rejection of the Holy Spirit’s work, treating the clear power and presence of God in Christ as demonic and refusing to repent.

35.x: Despite the slander of the Pharisees, Jesus doesn’t stop. This verse provides a summary of Jesus’ “Triple-Threat” ministry: (1) Teaching: explaining the scriptures (the Mind); (2) Preaching: proclaiming the good news of the kingdom (the Spirit); (3) Healing: restoring physical bodies (the Body). Note that he went to “all” cities and villages, he was thorough and inclusive, not just sticking to the big urban centers.

36.x: “Moved with compassion”: The Greek word used here (splagchnizomai) refers to a “gut-level” feeling. It’s not just pity; it’s a physical ache for the suffering of others. By calling them “sheep having no shepherd,” Jesus is issuing a silent indictment of the Pharisees. The religious leaders were supposed to be the shepherds of Israel, but instead of feeding the sheep, they were judging them and making their lives harder with legalism & man-made commandments (Mk 7:7-8).

37.x: Jesus looks at the crowds (the very ones who were “fainting and scattered”) and sees them not as a burden, but as a harvest. The harvest “truly is plenteous”: This represents the millions of souls ready to receive the gospel. It suggests that the problem isn’t a lack of interest from the world, but a lack of capacity from the church. Labourers are few: This is the crisis. A harvest that isn’t gathered will rot in the field. Jesus is pointing out that his own physical presence in one body isn’t enough to reach everyone; he needs “labourers” to join the effort.

38.x: The Lord of the Harvest is God the Father, the only true God (Jn 17:3). His human Son is praying to the divine omnipresent Spirit for help, and encourages others to do the same. If Jesus was God-the-Son (as Trinitarians claim), why does he need to pray to another divine person for help? A God, by definition, is the one prayed to, not the one praying to someone else. “He will send forth labourers”: The Greek word for “send forth” is ekballo, which literally means “to thrust out” or “to hurl.” It’s a strong word, implying that being a labourer for God often requires a divine push.

5-6.x: Saying “Your sins are forgiven” (BSB) is easy to say because it’s impossible to verify with the human eye. However, saying “Arise, and walk” is “harder” to say because if the man stays on the ground, the speaker is exposed as a fraud. Jesus performs the visible miracle (healing the paralysis) to prove he has authority to perform the invisible one (forgiving the soul). He uses the title “Son of Man,” a reference to the messianic figure in Daniel 7 who is given eternal dominion.

29-31.x: “According to your faith”: This is the key principle in Matthew. The “measure” of the miracle is linked to the “measure” of their faith. Jesus “straitly charged” (sternly warned) them to keep it quiet. Why? Likely because the term “Son of David” had political connotations. If the crowds got too excited, they might try to force him to be a political revolutionary against Rome before his time. However, while their excitement is understandable, their disobedience shows that while they had great faith, they still lacked submission to his timing.
